items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: Little Louie heard the records of the original Dixieland Jazz Band... Louis Armstrong in his book, Satchmo... listening to some new records I had just bought. New releases of the original Dixieland jazz band

ctx.x: Before who was this came to be?

I mean Clarence Williams. You got me right that time because I'm making a mistake. I'm just telling you, I'm reading. I'm not reading. I'm telling you from my mind. Clarence Williams came to New York around 1923. The first white man he met on Broadway was me with an introduction from A.J. Perron, which you'll find in their books too. And this Negro is supposed to have her buddy bowling play. Now let me tell you about this man, who he is, where he come from. If any of you serious scholars doubt me, I was just…

All right. This is a letter dated May the 27th, 1958 from Don Fowler, 9441 Southwest 8th Drive, Portland 1, Oregon. It's to D. James, D. The other day I ran across an interesting statement by Louis Armstrong in his book, Satchmo. He is discussing his life in New Orleans in 1918, and this is a paragraph. items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-10-26
items.q: And the same as Louis Armstrong's attack.

ctx.x: I don't know. Do you have any pieces among the ones that you haven't published, which might be described as jazz pieces in the sense that Tiger Rag and pieces like that?

Yes, I've got others. I don't see it as good as Tiger Rag, but there's one in here that has a very good jazz number. And this Let's Jam It has plausibilities. Even this one that I put out as a popular number can be played in the same idiom that I would play it. And so on. There's nothing to it. Any tune becomes a jazz tune when you put the idioms to it.…

These people tell you it's a great big secret. It's nothing but march time, syncopated. White man's music and not colored. That's all it is. You take the tiger rank, we'll fit in that. You play. Hold that tiger. Hold that tiger. You can do anything you want with it. It's waking up different embellishments on a chord construction. That's all it is. Now these fellas in New Orleans, they play today. You know who they play? I'm going to let you know who they play. They're great. I was nobody. They play Big…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: I had read that article that someone sent me, that Louis Armstrong had an arm full of records and he was listening to them, and he copied from them.

ctx.x: Well, we forgot about Lytel and Frankie Signorelli. About 1920, Signorelli joined my band. At that time they may have had a Memphis Five, but I never heard of them stopping the machine. Well, I had a little bit of friction with Roberson. He had promised the band a thousand dollars if I put Margie over. Well, I saw the plug of Margie for him, sang it for him, placed it on the record for him, and after he got his first statement, he didn't say anything. I asked him about what he was going to do to three of them.…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: The interviewee mentions Louis Armstrong in the context of recording with the Clarence Williams' Blue Five: 'Clarence Williams' Blue Five and the Clarence Williams' Blue Rhythm Band, which was featuring Louis Armstrong...'

ctx.x: Well, Paul Whiteman, Kid Tua Jazz. Mamie Smith and her jazz hands. I have them records of all of them. Clarence Williams' Blue Five and the Clarence Williams' Blue Rhythm Band, which was featuring Louis Armstrong, Donald Redmond, that's spelled R-E-D-M-O-N-D, Busta Bailey, Coleman Hawkins, etc. Louis Armstrong's first record that brought him recognition was Everybody Loves My Baby, which he recorded with the Clarence Williams' Blue Five. Fletcher Henderson and Benny Morton of Kansas City were also...
They were imitators of the Dixieland Jazz Band. Fletcher Henderson was one of the first colored men to copy from the records of the Dixieland Jazz Band.
